name: Ivan Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach science to twelve to fourteen-year-olds at Fernley Valley School, which serves about nine villages and a lot of farms, so half my kids come in on a bus at seven forty. My day is three practicals if I'm lucky: Bunsen burners, pond samples, a dissected owl pellet. I use an AI assistant every morning to rough out lesson plans and differentiated worksheets, which saves me an hour. What wears me out is the forty-minute drive each way and the fact that I'm the only physics-trained person in the building.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside school, how are things money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Jo, who runs the mobile library van for the county, so between us we know every pothole in the valley. I'm on lower pay because Fernley is a small school with no extra allowances, and we've got a car loan on the little hatchback I drive to work. Savings are about three weeks of bills. The nearest other secondary school is an hour away, so if I lost this job, I'd be moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a decent assistant, nothing more, and I'd tell colleagues which tools are actually worth it. I'd probably write a short post for the teachers' forum about what saved time and what didn't. I'd stay positive about it, because I've got real hours back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for the job but it doesn't touch the real problem, which is that I'm paid less than teachers in town and drive eighty minutes a day. Plateau or not, the car loan is still there and Jo's van route keeps getting threatened by council cuts. That's what keeps me up, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the planning tools and push the school to pay for a proper licence instead of my free account. I'd ask the head about the science lead allowance again, because that's another two thousand a year. And I'd keep doing the two evenings of online tutoring I already do, which covers the car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit flat. Like a lesson that goes to plan, but the plan was only ever okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Jo's route keeps getting threatened. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The county reviews the mobile library every budget, and every year the van survives by a few votes. If my partner Jo lost the library van, we'd lose a third of our income and the valley would lose its only library. People in the hamlets rely on that van for more than books, there's a woman who gets her blood pressure leaflets from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the hour AI saves you each morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I spend it setting up practicals properly, which is the whole point of science. Kids remember the day the owl pellet had a whole mouse skull in it. They don't remember the worksheet.

I'd write a **forum post** for other teachers, staying positive about it.

His partner's **library van** route is threatened by council cuts every year.

Push the head again for the **science lead allowance**.

feel: Mostly **fine** but a bit flat, like a lesson that only ever had an okay plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for teachers and unions to shape the tools instead of having them dropped on us. I'd volunteer to lead the staff training at Fernley, because somebody has to and I'm the one already using it. I'd also say loudly that time saved should go to kids, not to bigger classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in a better spot than most, because I already know these tools and science has a hands-on side. But I worry the county will use it as an excuse to merge small schools like ours, with one teacher doing remote lessons for three sites. And Jo's van is exactly the kind of service a council would swap for an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the AI training at school and ask for it to count towards a pay allowance. I'd join the union's technology committee to push for an agreement that saved time can't be used to cut staff. And I'd start a small paid newsletter for rural science teachers on using AI in practicals, maybe five pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but energised. It's like the first week of a new school year, a bit scary and a bit exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said time saved should go to kids. What if the county disagrees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's a fight, and that's what the union's for. I'd bring the numbers, hours saved, and show what we did with them. Councillors respond to spreadsheets more than speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about any colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our office manager, Bev, does timetables, bus lists and parent letters, which is the first list on that card. She's fifty-eight and has never sent an email without printing it first. I'd want to help her learn the tools before someone decides she's not needed.

I'd insist **time saved** goes to kids, not bigger classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for schools, and the government needs to guarantee teachers and kids a human in the room. I'd still say use the tools, but with rules. I'd be out with the union, and I'd be writing to the local MP every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 the AI does my planning, my marking and my explaining better than me, and that's most of what a teacher is paid for. The practicals and keeping kids safe in a lab last until robots arrive in 2031. So I think I'd have about three years as a lab supervisor on less pay, and then I don't know. With three weeks in the bank and a car loan, that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start retraining straight away for something hands-on and local, maybe as a lab technician or in farm tech, since the valley's full of farms that will need people to run the new kit. I'd pay off the car loan with every spare pound. Jo and I would talk about moving to a town where there's more than one kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, sharp and awake. I'd be doing a lot, which helps, but it's that feeling of running for a bus you might not catch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd retrain. With two years, what would that look like on a Monday morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching all day, then two evenings a week on a farm technology course online. Weekends shadowing the agricultural contractor who services the milking robots at Hendry's dairy. I'd basically have two jobs for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots change how you see your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. It means the hands-on bit of my job, the lab, is the bit that buys me time. A robot setting up thirty Bunsen burners safely with teenagers around is a long way off, even by 2031.

say: I'd say the government must guarantee a **human** in the room for children.
I'd keep backing the tools, but **with rules**, and write to the local MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's write the rules now: AI in schools with a teacher in charge, and funded retraining for anyone whose job changes. I'd be pushing the union to negotiate early, not wait for 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is actually enough time for me. I'd be thirty-two, already using these tools, and I could become the person who runs the AI side of science teaching across several rural schools. The risk is that job doesn't exist and they just cut teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch the county on a role as a digital science lead for the valley schools, part-time at first. I'd keep the tutoring and newsletter going and put the money into an emergency fund until I had two months saved. And I'd study a short course in data and education technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in control. Like a long hike where you can see the weather coming and you've got a waterproof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the county says no to that role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take it to the academy trusts in the city, they'd bite faster. Moving would be hard on Jo, because the library van is her whole life. But we've talked about it. My partner Jo said she'd rather move with a plan than stay with none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your students in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn to ask good questions and test answers, because that's science and that's also how you use AI well. And to get good with their hands, because the valley will still need people who can fix things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, and I'd want teachers involved in designing the AI that goes into classrooms. I'd be the annoying optimist in the staffroom, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years I think I'd do well out of it. I'd be thirty-seven, with a decade of AI experience, and schools will need people who can teach kids alongside these systems. The pay worry doesn't go away, but I'd have time to build up savings and skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the science lead role at Fernley, then a master's part-time in education technology over three or four years. I'd grow the newsletter into proper training for rural teachers. And I'd aim to have three months of savings by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, but mostly hopeful. It's like planting trees on the school field, you won't see them big for years but you know they're coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay worry doesn't go away. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even optimists pay rent, and small rural schools are always last for money. AI won't change that. A smaller profession could mean worse bargaining power for all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Jo's job be safe over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not as it is, the AI could do the catalogue and the advice, and a robot van in 2039. But Jo's good with people and knows every family in the valley. I'd want to help her plan too, not just me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd have the skills but not the time or the money to use them. What would help is the government paying teachers to retrain while still on salary, and a guarantee that small rural schools don't just get closed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about rural kids. If rural schools merge and go remote, kids on farms lose the one place they see thirty other kids every day. That matters more than test scores.

headlineQuote: If rural schools merge and go remote, kids on farms lose the one place they see thirty other kids every day.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** science teacher at a small rural school, living with his library-van partner.
He uses AI daily and wants to **lead the change** through training and the union.
Thin savings, a **car loan** and few nearby jobs keep him anxious when AGI comes fast.
He sees **lab practicals** as the hands-on part that buys him time.
With more warning he aims for a **digital science lead** role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have the skills but not the time or money.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** for teachers while still on salary.
A guarantee that **small rural schools** don't just close.
